newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl urged to lead but no quick fix in sight.
newsitem.headline: Kohl urged to lead but no quick fix in sight.

text.p: First the criticism came from Germany's opposition, then from his own party. Now even foreign partners have begun urging Chancellor Helmut Kohl to stand up and show convincing leadership.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, on a short visit to Germany on Monday, stopped short of mentioning Kohl's name when he bemoaned the difficulty Europe's powerhouse economy has meeting the criteria for the EU's planned single currency.
But his barbed remarks echoed what many German politicians have been saying for weeks -- that Kohl's solid consensus-style approach might not be fast enough to meet the challenges ahead.

The biggest one is whether Bonn, linchpin of the economic and monetary union (EMU), will actually qualify for it. Closely linked is the issue of whether Europe's leading statesman will be around to see through what could be a turbulent period.

"Germany has more political problems than economic problems," Prodi said in a jibe at the country most doubtful that Italy will qualify for EMU. "If Germany wanted, it could exercise the political leadership which is needed now."

But soaring unemployment and long-overdue economic reforms, the core of Kohl's problems as Bonn struggles to prepare for EMU, do not lend themselves to quick fixes -- especially not in cautious and thorough Germany.

Kohl's centre-right coalition decided on Tuesday against one headline-grabbing option, a proposed state spending freeze to keep the budget deficit from spilling over the three percent ceiling set in the Maastricht treaty.

Bonn has estimated its 1997 deficit at a precarious 2.9 percent of gross domestic product. But January's sudden rise unemployment to 4.66 million -- 12.2 percent of the workforce -- has cast deep doubt over that.

Kohl, who according to the German press is sliding into his "Kanzlerdaemmerung" (Twilight of the Chancellor), has also made clear he won't try to rally his troops with a dramatic gesture like announcing soon that he will run for reelection next year.

"I know my duty and I don't need any remedial help on this," Kohl, now 66 and in his 15th year in office, told the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung on Saturday. "I will make my decision known ... when I consider the time to be right."

Instead, officials in his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) said, Kohl is betting he can clear the Maastricht hurdle and regain his public standing by pushing through the long-overdue reforms of Germany's creaking tax and pension systems.
"The chancellor is dead set on pushing through these reforms," one official said. "Everything else is speculation."
Kohl has begun to move on tax cuts, a reform he says will lower high labour costs, boost investment and create jobs.

In an unusual move, he has invited the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to discuss options with him next Monday. While still far apart, the parties seem ready to compromise to make more tax cuts next year.
The outlook is less clear for pension reform, an emotional issue for Germany's "greying" population and a point of discord both in Kohl's cabinet and between government and opposition.

"No matter what he does here, he'll do something wrong -- that's why he's so unsure," one official said. "Either he cuts benefits and angers older voters or raises contributions and turns young people against him. There is no easy way out."

Overshadowing all of this is concern whether Bonn can bring down the jobless figures, its highest since 1933, or watch as extra unemployment benefits jack up government spending beyond the Maastricht ceiling.
Bonn has been dizzy with speculation about Kohl's future, the latest being that he would announce a reelection bid in early April after his annual Easter slimming vacation.
But Kohl himself seemed to rule that out last week when he said he would consider the issue after the June EU summit in Amsterdam that should seal the union's will to launch EMU.
A more likely occasion would be the CDU's annual congress in October, by which time unemployment should have receded a bit and the reforms could have at least taken shape.
Although nobody knows whether he will run, pollsters say his party has not suffered badly despite Germany's problems. The CDU is now level with the SPD at around 37 percent support.

"Despite a disastrous situation since the end of 1995, the CDU has only lost three percent of its voters while the SPD has simply regained support it lost after the 1994 election," Emnid's Klaus-Peter Schoeppner said.
